claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start the assessment process.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! To start, I need to know about the child (or children) you're claiming for.

**Could you please tell me:**
1. How many children do you want to claim Child Benefit for?
2. What are their names?
3. What are their ages (or dates of birth)?

This will help me determine which eligibility path applies to each child.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm looking to claim for my son Alex. He's 17 years old and lives at home with me.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! So you're looking to claim Child Benefit for your son Alex, who is 17 years old.

Since Alex is between 16 and 19 years old, there are additional requirements we need to check. Let me navigate to the appropriate section.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect. For young people aged 16-19 like Alex, there are specific requirements about education or training.

**Is Alex currently:**
1. **In approved education or training** (such as full-time non-advanced education like A-levels, Scottish Highers, NVQ Level 3, or approved vocational training), OR
2. **Has he recently left education or training** (within the last 20 weeks), OR
3. **Neither** - he's not in education/training and didn't recently leave?

Could you let me know which situation applies to Alex?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, Alex is currently in education - he's studying for his A-levels at sixth form college.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Since Alex is studying for his A-levels at sixth form college, let me check the education level requirements.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great news! A-levels at sixth form college is an approved non-advanced qualification for Child Benefit purposes. Now I need to check a few more details about Alex's education:

**1. Is Alex's course full-time?** (This means at least 12 hours per week of supervised study - classroom time, tutorials, etc. - not counting homework)

**2. Is this education funded by an employer or connected to an agreed future job with an employer?** (Most sixth form courses aren't, but I need to confirm)

Could you answer these two questions about Alex's A-level course?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, it's a full-time course at the sixth form college - he's there during the day like a regular school schedule. And no, it's not connected to any employer or job - it's just regular A-levels through the college.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! That's all very positive for eligibility. A-levels at sixth form college on a full-time basis are approved education for Child Benefit purposes.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent. Now I need to check Alex's work situation:

**Does Alex work less than 24 hours per week (or is he not in paid work at all)?**

This is important because young people aged 16-19 who work 24 hours or more per week are not eligible for Child Benefit, even if they're also in education.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Actually, Alex does work quite a bit - he has a part-time job at the supermarket where he works full-time hours alongside his studies. So yes, he works 24 hours or more per week, but he's still doing his A-levels as well.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I see. Thank you for being clear about that. Unfortunately, this is an important factor for eligibility.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I'm sorry to inform you that based on the information provided, **you would not be eligible for Child Benefit for Alex**.

**Here's why:**

Even though Alex is still studying for his A-levels (which is approved education), the rules state that young people aged 16 or over who work 24 or more hours per week are not eligible for Child Benefit. This applies even when they're also in education.

**Important to note:**

- If Alex reduces his working hours to less than 24 hours per week while continuing his A-level studies, you may become eligible to claim Child Benefit for him again
- Child Benefit eligibility could resume if his work situation changes

**What happens next:**

If Alex's working hours change in the future (for example, if he reduces to part-time hours under 24 hours per week), you can claim Child Benefit at that point.

Is there anything else you'd like to know about Child Benefit eligibility, or do you have questions about this decision?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Oh, I see. That's disappointing, but I understand - it's because he's working those full-time hours at the supermarket. Thank you for explaining that clearly. I suppose if he cuts back his hours during exam time or something, I could look into claiming then. I appreciate your help with this.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
You're very welcome, and I'm glad I could explain it clearly for you. Yes, that's exactly right - if Alex does reduce his hours to under 24 hours per week at any point (whether for exams or any other reason) while he's still doing his A-levels, you would be able to claim Child Benefit for him at that time.

Let me record the final outcome of this assessment:

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Summary of your assessment:**

- **Child:** Alex (age 17)
- **Result:** Not eligible for Child Benefit
- **Reason:** Working 24+ hours per week (even though in approved education)
- **Possible future eligibility:** If working hours reduce to under 24 hours per week while still in A-level studies

It's great that Alex is balancing both his studies and work - that shows a lot of dedication! Just keep in mind that option to claim if his circumstances change.

Best of luck to Alex with his A-levels, and don't hesitate to reach out if you have any other questions in the future!
